channel_name: Real Vision · Raoul Pal - The journey man
video_title: Why The Next Phase of Crypto Is Bigger Than You Think w/ Blue Macellari | Raoul Pal The Journey Man
gist: T. Rowe Price's head of digital assets, Blue Macellari, tells Raoul Pal that institutional plumbing for on-chain finance is finally in place — she has done 15-20 client board presentations on tokenization in six months at a $1.8tn asset manager — but that adoption will be 'experimental and then all at once,' not incremental, which explains why crypto prices have lagged despite the news flow. She argues the marginal high-growth-tech buyer rotated into AI equities (calling the SpaceX IPO buyer 'a Solana holder'), that tokenizing illiquid assets creates only 'the illusion of liquidity,' and that fragmented, non-interoperable stablecoins and terrible UX are the real adoption blockers. Both speakers spend a large block on AI risk and the unsolved on-chain digital-identity problem.

insights.claim: Blue Macellari, who runs digital assets at T. Rowe Price, has delivered roughly 15-20 board-level presentations on tokenization and stablecoins to large institutional clients in the past six months, having never been asked to do one before that.
insights.speaker: Blue Macellari, T. Rowe Price head of digital assets
insights.so_what: Board-level demand from corporate plan sponsors is a leading indicator of tokenized-product mandates; watch for RFPs and pilot allocations from 401k/retirement plan sponsors over the next 12 months.
insights.quote: I want to say over the past 6 months I have probably done 15 or 20 board presentations on tokenization and stablecoins.

insights.claim: T. Rowe Price manages roughly $1.8 trillion with a large share in retirement/401k assets, and the inbound tokenization interest is coming from the boards of those corporate retirement clients, independently of each other.
insights.speaker: Blue Macellari
insights.so_what: Retirement money is the largest untapped pool for on-chain products; simultaneous independent inbounds suggest a genuine demand wave rather than one salesperson's pipeline.
insights.quote: we're 1.8 trillion dollar asset manager. A large portion are retirement assets

insights.claim: Traditional finance is now approaching crypto to import crypto-native market functionality (perpetuals, prediction markets, Hyperliquid-style venues) into traditional markets, reversing the usual direction of technology transfer.
insights.speaker: Blue Macellari
insights.so_what: Crypto market-structure primitives, not just crypto assets, are the export product — favors venues and infra whose designs TradFi will license or copy.
insights.quote: I think that we have hit a point where much of traditional finance is beginning to understand and see the functionality that has developed in crypto markets that would be phenomenal to introduce to traditional markets.

insights.claim: Traditional hedge fund managers and CIOs who had gone silent for six months are cold-calling to ask about Hyperliquid, indicating discretionary TradFi capital is starting to research on-chain venues directly.
insights.speaker: Blue Macellari
insights.so_what: A soft signal that on-chain perp DEX volumes could see non-native flow; monitor Hyperliquid volume/fee capture as a proxy for TradFi curiosity converting to activity.
insights.quote: I hadn't spoken to them in 6 months." And they're like, "Hey, so I'm watching this hype. What what do you think about this hype stuff, you know?"

insights.claim: The regulatory unlock for active multi-token retail products was the arrival of generic listing standards about a year ago, not the original spot Bitcoin ETF approvals — T. Rowe had been trading 20+ tokens internally since 2023 with no path to market.
insights.speaker: Blue Macellari
insights.so_what: The bottleneck on altcoin ETF supply was listing standards; expect a wave of actively managed multi-token vehicles rather than more single-asset trusts.
insights.quote: by 2023 we were trading 20 plus tokens internally in a portfolio. But there just wasn't a a regulatory framework or a path to bringing something to market for retail.

insights.claim: T. Rowe Price built its digital-assets business as a fully crypto-native end-to-end stack that shares nothing with the firm's legacy systems except Microsoft Outlook.
insights.speaker: Blue Macellari
insights.so_what: Legacy asset managers cannot retrofit existing systems for crypto — the vendor spend goes to crypto-native custody, OMS and reconciliation providers, not incumbent fund-admin platforms.
insights.quote: We don't use any T Rowe existing systems except for Microsoft Outlook.

insights.claim: Conservative asset managers (Fidelity, T. Rowe, Franklin) persisted through the bear market while banks like Goldman and JPMorgan repeatedly built and shut crypto desks, because US regulation targeted banks and broker-dealers specifically while asset managers retained autonomy.
insights.speaker: Raoul Pal and Blue Macellari
insights.so_what: Asset managers, not banks, have the incumbent head start in on-chain distribution; bank re-entry is a catch-up trade rather than a leadership one.
insights.quote: the regulatory environment in the US became really hostile and it was very much directed towards banks and asset managers still had a lot of freedom and autonomy

insights.claim: The marginal buyer of high-growth tech risk rotated out of crypto into AI equities over the past year, with the SpaceX IPO absorbing capital that would previously have gone to tokens.
insights.speaker: Blue Macellari
insights.so_what: Crypto beta is now competing directly with private/public AI equity issuance for the same speculative dollar — track AI IPO calendars as a drain on altcoin flows.
insights.quote: I think that marginal buyer of the SpaceX IPO is like a Solana holder. I absolutely think that.

insights.claim: Crypto came off a 'sugar high' of unprecedented positive news flow that ran from the first spot Bitcoin ETFs through last summer, and the market is now suffering from the mathematical impossibility of sustaining that pace of transformational headlines rather than from deteriorating fundamentals.
insights.speaker: Blue Macellari
insights.so_what: Frames the drawdown as a news-flow air pocket, not a thesis break — argues for accumulating rather than de-risking if you share the view.
insights.quote: it's impossible to sustain that type of constant transformational um news flow

insights.claim: Nobody in the crypto industry has produced a convincing explanation for the October 10 liquidation event, and the absence of subsequent bankruptcies is itself the notable data point — no 'bodies floated to the surface' unlike prior cycles.
insights.speaker: Blue Macellari
insights.so_what: No hidden leverage cascade means the overhang is sentiment and liquidity, not solvency — reduces tail risk of a forced-selling second leg down.
insights.quote: I don't feel like we really understand as a community what happened 10 10.

insights.claim: Excess liquidity — defined as liquidity growth above GDP growth — has not been strong, so the limited marginal capital available concentrated in the single highest-returning attention sink, AI, starving crypto of the reflexive price-begets-volume loop.
insights.speaker: Raoul Pal
insights.so_what: A reusable macro screen: crypto needs excess liquidity, not just liquidity — watch liquidity-minus-nominal-GDP as the trigger for the next crypto beta window.
insights.quote: I look at sort of excess liquidity which is liquidity growth above GDP growth and it hasn't been very strong

insights.claim: The industry over-promised on 'institutions are coming' and crypto markets, which are not patient, punished the gap when institutional arrival failed to translate into measurable on-chain throughput.
insights.speaker: Blue Macellari
insights.so_what: Use network throughput and fee data — not press releases — as the real confirmation signal before paying up for institutional-adoption narratives.
insights.quote: institutions are here, institutions are building. We're just not fast, right? Um, and and crypto markets are not necessarily that patient.

insights.claim: Mainstream AI equity exposure is still concentrated almost entirely in the core-infrastructure and hardware narrative, with the application layer not yet understood or priced by the marginal buyer.
insights.speaker: Blue Macellari
insights.so_what: Implies the AI application layer is the under-owned leg, and that the crypto-AI intersection only gets repriced after the infra trade matures.
insights.quote: the taxi driver told me to buy Nvidia. Like, it's that sort of top layer of things, you have to let it mature

insights.claim: AI agents structurally require crypto rails because machines cannot hold or transact in conventional bank dollars, expanding crypto's addressable market from roughly 8 billion humans to an unbounded number of agents.
insights.speaker: Blue Macellari and Raoul Pal
insights.so_what: The agentic-payments TAM argument is the strongest long-horizon bull case articulated here; watch agent payment protocols and stablecoin settlement volume as the KPI.
insights.quote: the TAM of of crypto has gone from 8 billion people to infinite agents

insights.claim: Tokenizing illiquid assets creates accessibility and the illusion of liquidity but does not manufacture liquidity where none exists, making 'unlocking illiquid asset classes' the weakest argument for tokenization.
insights.speaker: Blue Macellari
insights.so_what: Be skeptical of tokenized illiquid-asset platforms marketed on liquidity; the historical pattern of forcing liquidity onto illiquid underlyings ends in blowups.
insights.quote: it brings greater accessibility and the illusion of greater liquidity, but it doesn't actually create liquidity where there is none

insights.claim: A structural mismatch exists in tokenized private markets: sponsors who have run out of buyers for private credit and real estate want to tokenize to reach retail, while retail has shown no genuine demand to own a fractional token of an illiquid building.
insights.speaker: Raoul Pal
insights.so_what: Treat retail-distributed tokenized private assets as supply-driven, not demand-driven — a classic sign of late-cycle product-pushing.
insights.quote: I've never met a real estate guy who has not said, "I'm interested in tokenization" but on the other side I've never met a retail investor who really cares about buying tokens on a share of some illiquid building

insights.claim: Tokenized wrappers around gated, quarterly-redemption funds create a hidden hazard: buyers assume blockchain delivery changes the underlying terms, and packaged economic interests traded on secondary markets with unknown NAVs plus looping leverage become a 'powder keg' of unrecognized counterparty risk.
insights.speaker: Blue Macellari
insights.so_what: A specific, identifiable systemic-risk vector to watch in the next crypto credit event: leveraged secondary markets on tokenized gated funds.
insights.quote: Especially when you're introduced, right? Like infinite looping, but then it becomes like a real powder keg.

insights.claim: Private equity and alternatives portfolio managers actively do not want daily mark-to-market or to send investor letters to holders who owned a token for 30 seconds, so PMs themselves are likely to push back against tokenizing their funds.
insights.speaker: Blue Macellari
insights.so_what: Internal PM resistance, not regulation, may be the binding constraint on tokenized private funds — a supply-side brake most bulls ignore.
insights.quote: if you talk to a portfolio manager at a private equity fund or an alternatives fund, they do not want their stuff to mark to market daily

insights.claim: The core economic function of private-market vehicles is presenting a zero-volatility reported structure over volatile underlying assets, and that smoothing is itself the arbitrage being sold.
insights.speaker: Raoul Pal
insights.so_what: Explains why on-chain transparency is existentially threatening to alternatives fee models — an under-discussed reason tokenization stalls in that segment.
insights.quote: It is to have a zero volatility structure with things that actually volatile underneath is is the arbitrage.

insights.claim: The right tokenization sequence is liquid first: fixed income and yield products, then all equities and anything homogeneous, with illiquid real estate explicitly last rather than first.
insights.speaker: Raoul Pal
insights.so_what: A practical filter for picking tokenization winners: favor platforms attacking liquid, homogeneous assets over illiquid-asset marketplaces.
insights.quote: All of equities, anything basically homogeneous should be on chain. It's the fastest, most efficient way of transferring and custodying assets

insights.claim: Tokenization-as-a-service has collapsed the cost curve so far that what required roughly $15 million, 100 people and two and a half years four years ago can now be assembled on a platform like Securitize in a configurator-style flow.
insights.speaker: Blue Macellari
insights.so_what: Commoditized issuance means no moat in the tokenizing itself — value accrues to distribution and to whoever answers 'who is this product for,' not to the tech vendor.
insights.quote: you could now tokenize something what would have cost you 15 million dollars, 100 people in 2 and 1/2 years to do 4 years ago

insights.claim: Because issuance is now cheap, tokenization has become a business strategy question rather than a technology or operations question — the binding decision is who you are trying to reach and what they actually want.
insights.speaker: Blue Macellari
insights.so_what: Screening heuristic for tokenization ventures: those without a defined end-buyer are supply looking for demand and likely to fail.
insights.quote: It's not a tech conversation. It's a business strategy conversation.

insights.claim: Migration of mainstream markets on-chain will not be incremental — it must run as sidecar pilots because live market plumbing cannot be tinkered with, then flip all at once once dozens of broker-dealers and asset managers agree industry standards.
insights.speaker: Blue Macellari
insights.so_what: Implies a long flat period followed by a step-change — linear extrapolation of current on-chain volumes will badly underestimate the eventual jump.
insights.quote: it's it's not going to be fast and it is not going to be incremental. It will be experimental and then sort of all at once.

insights.claim: 24/7 US equity trading is only technically feasible on-chain, and the DTCC's clearing volumes represent the scale of demand headed for block space.
insights.speaker: Blue Macellari and Raoul Pal
insights.so_what: Links a concrete, already-announced TradFi initiative (round-the-clock equities) to blockspace demand — the cleanest bridge between equity market reform and L1/L2 revenue.
insights.quote: All anybody wants to talk about is how we're getting to 24/7 trading in, like, US equities. And guess what? Like, you know how that's going to happen? It's got to be on-chain because it it's just not feasible.

themes.theme: Interoperability and UX as the real blocker

insights.claim: The stablecoin market is fragmenting into permissioned chains, open-source chains and multi-chain deployments, breaking the one thing stablecoins were supposed to do — make sending a dollar trivially easy.
insights.speaker: Raoul Pal
insights.so_what: Fragmentation risk argues against betting on any single issuer's walled garden and toward abstraction/routing layers.
insights.quote: we're kind of losing the interoperability because people are trying to capture market share without realizing you'll all have market share, just let it grow

insights.claim: Stablecoins today resemble the cable-to-streaming transition — fragmented across services no consumer can track — and the eventual market leader will be whoever abstracts away bridging and back-end complexity entirely.
insights.speaker: Blue Macellari
insights.so_what: Points investment toward the aggregation/abstraction layer rather than individual stablecoin issuers or chains.
insights.quote: the winner is going to be the person who is able to abstract away the back end and bridging and all of the things that crypto people are willing to do that the average consumer is not

insights.claim: Everyone who will ever reach crypto through code or hardcore tech has already arrived, so all remaining growth depends on products built for non-technical users — a saturation argument that reframes UX from nice-to-have to the only growth lever.
insights.speaker: Blue Macellari
insights.so_what: The developer-and-degen addressable market is tapped out; consumer-app quality is now the entire adoption function.
insights.quote: everybody who is going to get here through code is already here. Everybody who is going to get here through like sort of hardcore tech, they're already here.

insights.claim: TradFi asset managers have yet to learn the lesson prior crypto cycles taught — that different blockchains suit different purposes and a walled-garden land grab cannot sustain the space.
insights.speaker: Blue Macellari
insights.so_what: Expect a costly detour through proprietary institutional chains before consolidation onto interoperable public infrastructure.
insights.quote: a real estate land grab walled garden, doesn't work

insights.claim: The industry's separation of 'crypto' from 'tokenization' in TradFi conversations is incoherent, because a multi-trillion-dollar stablecoin market is by definition demand for block space paid for in crypto.
insights.speaker: Blue Macellari
insights.so_what: The direct trade expression of stablecoin growth is the underlying chains' fee/token economics, not the stablecoin issuers alone.
insights.quote: We think that there's going to be call it a trillion, call it five trillion, whatever your number is on stable coins, but like that's block space, right?

insights.claim: Blockchain is not the right tool for everything — it is specifically suited to things that are complex, difficult, or must be securely moved, transferred and represented across internal and external parties; plenty else belongs in a database.
insights.speaker: Blue Macellari
insights.so_what: A crisp screen for evaluating enterprise blockchain pitches — cross-party representation and transfer, or it is database theater.
insights.quote: Blockchain is fantastic for anything that is complex, difficult um or needs to be securely moved, transferred, and represented across internal and external parties

insights.claim: The recurring systemic error in crypto is that firms monitor their direct counterparty but not their counterparty's counterparty, the same failure seen at Long-Term Capital Management where everyone's biggest client was the same client — and in 2022 that shared client was Three Arrows Capital.
insights.speaker: Raoul Pal and Blue Macellari
insights.so_what: A reusable diligence question for any lending or prime-brokerage exposure: map the second-degree counterparty concentration, not just the first.
insights.quote: everybody's biggest client was Three Arrows Capital and nobody knew

insights.claim: A market where a large share of participants are retail on auto-liquidation adds non-linear surprise to crises, because positions flip without the holder's knowledge and the exit door shrinks exactly when everyone runs for it.
insights.speaker: Blue Macellari
insights.so_what: Explains crypto's gap risk profile and why liquidity metrics measured in calm markets systematically overstate available exit capacity.
insights.quote: when you have a massive system that in large part a big portion of it is retail operating on auto liquidation, it just like it adds a bunch of surprises to the mix

insights.claim: Architecture built before a crisis paid off: T. Rowe's crypto setup would have had price exposure to the FTX-era drawdown but zero counterparty or vendor exposure through the entire December-January bankruptcy daisy chain.
insights.speaker: Blue Macellari
insights.so_what: Concrete proof that segregated custody architecture is the differentiator for institutional crypto mandates — a diligence checklist item, not a marketing line.
insights.quote: we would have had zero counterparty exposure or vendor exposure

insights.claim: Most crypto firms that failed lacked risk managers who had personally lived through an everybody-heads-for-the-door crisis, a gap that EM, macro and distressed veterans fill naturally.
insights.speaker: Blue Macellari
insights.so_what: Team-composition signal when underwriting crypto funds or exchanges: look for crisis-tested risk leadership, not just crypto-native credentials.

insights.claim: EM FX and commodity traders adapt to crypto fastest because gap risk, illiquidity, volatility, information asymmetry and skew are the same skill set, with FX traders picking it up quickest of all.
insights.speaker: Raoul Pal and Blue Macellari
insights.so_what: Useful lens for evaluating crypto trading teams — and for treating crypto as a frontier/EM asset class rather than a tech equity.
insights.quote: I always think that the people who pick it up the fastest are like our FX guys

insights.claim: The single most expensive trait in investing is rigidity — Macellari cites her Elliott CIO's maxim and Pal describes having to abandon a career-long bear-market bias to trade the technology trend.
insights.speaker: Blue Macellari (citing her Elliott Management CIO) and Raoul Pal
insights.so_what: A meta-lesson on process: track record in one regime is a liability if it hardens into a prior; both speakers had to invert their frameworks to stay relevant.
insights.quote: the most expensive thing you can be in our business is rigid

insights.claim: Crypto tokens are the first truly 100% fungible spot commodities tradable simultaneously anywhere in the world, making crypto arguably the only genuinely market-neutral asset class — unlike wheat or oil, which vary by grade and geography.
insights.speaker: Blue Macellari
insights.so_what: Structural argument for why cross-exchange arb and basis trades in crypto are cleaner than in physical commodities — relevant to allocating to market-neutral crypto managers.
insights.quote: they are the very first truly 100% fungible spot commodities that can be traded simultaneously anywhere in the world

themes.theme: AI risk and the unsolved identity layer

insights.claim: Pal convened senior people from Amazon, Meta, LinkedIn/Microsoft and Google in 2021 to build a common on-chain digital identity standard; all agreed AI made it urgent, and all refused to accept each other's credentials, so nothing was built.
insights.speaker: Raoul Pal
insights.so_what: Big Tech interoperability refusal is the structural reason on-chain identity remains an open market — and a legal liability building toward post-2008-style litigation.
insights.quote: We'd love to, but we're never going to agree each other's credentials.

insights.claim: Digital identity and provenance should be the top priority given AI-generated fake content, yet nobody is talking about it properly and the Web3 'rewrite/own' narrative has stalled alongside it.
insights.speaker: Raoul Pal and Blue Macellari
insights.so_what: An explicitly under-invested vertical both speakers flag as critical — a potential asymmetric area for early positioning in identity/provenance protocols.
insights.quote: I just don't understand how we're not more you know, more focused on identity and verification

insights.claim: AI safety currently rests on voluntary self-reporting by labs, and Macellari says she does not have the trust that requires while also seeing no feasible or coherent path to government-level regulation.
insights.speaker: Blue Macellari
insights.so_what: A senior institutional allocator publicly discounting the AI governance regime — relevant to how the buy side will eventually price AI regulatory/tail risk.
insights.quote: there's a huge element of trust there that I don't I personally am don't really have at this point

insights.claim: An Imperial War College study of AI models in war-game simulations found that nine out of ten times models escalated to nuclear weapons within three or four steps, and inputting civilian casualty constraints did not change the outcome across models.
insights.speaker: Blue Macellari
insights.so_what: The specific evidence driving an institutional PM's AI pessimism — an alignment failure mode that is model-agnostic and unresponsive to prompt-level ethical constraints.
insights.quote: That's like becomes the optimal outcome is always they just like go straight for the nuclear weapons.

insights.claim: AI capability is compounding on a Reed's law curve rather than crypto's Metcalfe's law, with intelligence-output efficiency doubling roughly every five months and a new frontier model every two weeks, making government regulation structurally impossible.
insights.speaker: Raoul Pal
insights.so_what: If the doubling rate is right, capability-based valuation models for AI need a far steeper curve than the adoption curves investors imported from crypto or the internet.
insights.quote: compounding um intelligence is compounding uh it's like doubling every 5 months uh the efficiency of intelligence output

insights.claim: Pal argues the AI race is unstoppable on game-theory grounds because the prize is enormous — citing Anthropic as the fastest-scaling revenue company in human history — and because it is layered on top of US-versus-China competition.
insights.speaker: Raoul Pal
insights.so_what: Rules out a regulatory-slowdown scenario in AI capex forecasts — the base case is continued acceleration regardless of safety concerns.
insights.quote: Anthropic is the largest, fastest scaling of revenues in any company in human history

insights.claim: Pal expects AGI embodied in robots — smarter, stronger, faster, cheaper intelligence with dexterity, scalable beyond current comprehension — roughly three years out.
insights.speaker: Raoul Pal
insights.so_what: A concrete near-term timeline from a macro investor for the humanoid-robotics thesis; if credible, labor-cost-sensitive sectors reprice well before 2030.
insights.quote: We've birthed intelligence that is beyond our own. And we're going to put AGI into physical form, into robots.

themes.theme: Retail distribution and the Robinhood squeeze

insights.claim: Robinhood under Vlad Tenev is simultaneously attacking crypto, wealth management and asset management, and its speed is forcing Coinbase and traditional shops to accelerate — Pal calls Coinbase slow for an organization that should be nimble.
insights.speaker: Raoul Pal and Blue Macellari
insights.so_what: Competitive-pressure read: Robinhood is the pace-setter and Coinbase the laggard on product velocity — relevant to relative positioning between the two.
insights.quote: they're transforming like both sides of the aisle. So, like they're coming like they're coming for everybody

insights.claim: Study after study shows that as cohorts skew younger, first financial experience is digital and they hold more digital assets than mutual funds — a demographic split between traditional brokerage accounts and fintech apps.
insights.speaker: Blue Macellari
insights.so_what: Long-run structural flow argument for digital-asset AUM at the expense of mutual fund complexes as generational wealth transfer proceeds.

insights.claim: The product design question T. Rowe is focused on is what investors who expect 24/7 on-chain trading and instant settlement actually want to own — people who call in confused when a mutual fund purchase takes three days.
insights.speaker: Blue Macellari
insights.so_what: Settlement expectations, not asset preference, will drive product redesign at incumbents — watch for instant-settlement fund wrappers as the competitive response.

insights.claim: Legacy financial rails will not disappear even as usage collapses — banks will maintain paper check capability for decades because you cannot mothball infrastructure customers still occasionally use, meaning on-chain and legacy systems run in parallel far longer than crypto natives expect.
insights.speaker: Blue Macellari
insights.so_what: Argues against 'replacement' theses and for coexistence — costs stay in the system, so disruption shows up in new-flow share rather than incumbent revenue collapse.
insights.quote: it is still going to be probably decades before banks eliminate that capability even though nobody uses it

themes.theme: The untapped corporate treasury and commodity-trading opportunity

insights.claim: Global commodity trading houses with capital trapped across jurisdictions like Angola, Tanzania and French Guiana and facing capital controls are the most obvious untapped users of internal stablecoin rails, yet adoption has not happened at scale.
insights.speaker: Raoul Pal
insights.so_what: An identified, unserved enterprise TAM — a go-to-market wedge for stablecoin infrastructure providers and a signal to watch for the first large commodity-house deployment.
insights.quote: they might as well just have an internal stablecoin rails and they can move money around from entity to entity, no problem. And I'm surprised that's not happened at scale yet.

insights.claim: Macellari's direct check with the LatAm head trader at a very large commodities firm confirmed nobody there is even evaluating stablecoins — the gap is not a slow rollout, it is total absence of internal discussion.
insights.speaker: Blue Macellari
insights.so_what: Primary-source evidence that enterprise stablecoin adoption in commodities is at zero, not early — resets timelines for anyone underwriting that revenue line.
insights.quote: he's like, "Nope. Nope, we're not. Nobody's looking at it."

insights.claim: Sell-side banks are the likely blocker on corporate stablecoin adoption because their coverage teams earn from currency options and cash-management products, and pitching stablecoins would cannibalize their own business.
insights.speaker: Blue Macellari and Raoul Pal
insights.so_what: Identifies distribution — not technology or regulation — as the constraint; adoption likely comes from non-bank fintechs going direct to corporate treasurers.
insights.quote: Well, because you make more money selling currency options.

insights.claim: Working smart-contract precedents already exist and are being ignored: Louis Dreyfus and other soft-commodity houses moved letters of credit and shipping documentation onto smart contracts around 2016-2017, and Citi ran trade finance where GPS oracle confirmation of a canal transit triggered release of financing.
insights.speaker: Raoul Pal and Blue Macellari
insights.so_what: Proof-of-concept risk is already retired in trade finance — the failure to scale is organizational, which means adoption could be fast once one major house moves.

insights.claim: Historical capital-control arbitrages — Cargill using equity index arb to extract trapped South African rand under the dual financial/commercial rand system, and Argentina's blue chip swap — are exactly the frictions stablecoins now solve at near-zero cost.
insights.speaker: Raoul Pal and Blue Macellari
insights.so_what: Sizes the value pool by pointing at the elaborate legacy workarounds corporates already pay for — stablecoin savings equal the entire fee stack of those arbitrages.

insights.claim: Brazil is unusually crypto-forward relative to its recognition and has already begun using stablecoin-style rails for corporate money movement.
insights.speaker: Raoul Pal and Blue Macellari
insights.so_what: Brazil as the live test market for enterprise stablecoin adoption — a place to observe the template before it generalizes.
insights.quote: Brazil is actually unbelievably crypto forward.
